title: Future of Intertidal Habitats in the Pilbara
text: Overview

title: Future of Intertidal Habitats in the Pilbara
text:
Scope of the Project


As part of Project B (Quantifying the effects of climate change on intertidal habitats of the west Pilbara coast) of the WAMSI Mardie Offset Marine and Intertidal Research Program, this project aims to improve understanding of how intertidal habitats along the West Pilbara coast may respond to future environmental change and/or development pressures. The project develops an integrated modelling framework to investigate the potential effects of sea-level rise, hydrodynamic variability, and coastal development pressures on key intertidal benthic communities and habitats, including mangroves, cyanobacterial mats, and salt-flat environments.
The project focuses on understanding how changes in inundation patterns, water depth and coastal processes may influence the future distribution and persistence of intertidal habitats. The modelling framework provides a tool to explore potential future scenarios and assess the capacity of these ecosystems to adapt under changing environmental conditions as well as development impacts.








Figure 1: Photo of the Urala site – representative photo showing the zonation of intertidal habitats: mangroves, algal mats (Photo courtesy: Toby Brown).

title: Future of Intertidal Habitats in the Pilbara
text:
Major Findings

Modelling Capability & Framework Advancement
One of the key outcomes of this project is the development of a coupled eco-geomorphic modelling framework capable of simulating across coastal scales \(O(\text{km})\).

Advancement Over Existing Approaches: While existing approaches have demonstrated three-way coupling between bio-hydromorphodynamics, they remain limited to idealised domains or relatively small, localised areas. In this work, we have advanced these capabilities to implement a three-way coupling framework at regional coastal scales. The new framework integrates fine-scale hydrodynamic, sediment transport, and habitat response dynamics, allowing explicit simulation of non-linear responses such as non-monotonic mangrove expansion and physical habitat compression. For more details, readers are referred to Chapter 3.
Transferability: The framework is modular and scalable. It can be directly applied to other coastal sites globally, provided it is calibrated and adapted for site-specific sea-level rise and climate scenarios, as well as environmental impact assessments (EIAs) for coastal infrastructure and resource development projects.

The modelling results highlight the critical importance of evaluating coupled physical-ecological interactions when assessing future coastal change. While coastal infrastructure and development footprints may restrict local habitat migration pathways, these insights provide a broader understanding of long-term habitat trajectories to support improved spatial planning and management strategies across Pilbara coastal ecosystems.






Figure 2: Drone video of the Urala intertidal site captured during baseline surveys of WAMSI fieldwork April 2024 (Urala Study site, Pilbara, WA; Source: Toby Brown).





Modelling Outcomes






ImportantKey Question: How Do Specific Intertidal Habitats Adapt to Rising Sea Levels?



Do Mangroves Survive Sea-Level Rise (SLR)?
Yes, but only up to a threshold. Under high SLR scenarios, mangroves initially expand landward rather than immediately retreating. This follows a non-monotonic “expansion followed by drowning” trajectory:

Phase 1 (Landward Expansion): Mangroves encroach landward into higher bed elevations (shifting upward from ~1.0 m to 2.5 m elevation).
Phase 2 (Drowning & Die-back): Once the rate of SLR outpaces the rate of sediment accretion, severe drowning and tree mortality occur.


Do Algal Mats Survive Sea-Level Rise (SLR)?
Yes, but they cannot maintain their current spatial footprint. Algal mats survive primarily by migrating landward into higher-elevation supratidal zones:

Landward Encroachment: As sea levels rise, expanding mangrove communities colonise former algal mat territory.
Habitat Squeezing: To stay within their ideal inundation window, algal mats are forced into higher elevations (above 2.5 m elevation).
Spatial Compression: This landward migration drastically squeezes their overall area, restricting remaining algal mats to narrow fringe bands at the landward edge of the coastal profile.









NoteKey Question: Do Intertidal Habitats Survive Future Sea-Level Rise?



Overview of Trajectories and Coastal Squeezing
The modelling assessment indicates that rising sea levels will drive significant shifts in the distribution and extent of intertidal habitats through altered inundation regimes. While response trajectories vary sharply by habitat type based on their specific elevation thresholds and adaptive limits, the overarching result across the profile is a shift from species die-off at seaward boundaries to migration and spatial squeeze at landward margins.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Coastal Habitats and How They Change
Coastal intertidal habitats including mangroves, saltmarshes (samphires), cyanobacterial (algal) mats, and saltflats are dynamic eco-geomorphic systems shaped by continuous feedbacks between hydrodynamic forcing, sediment dynamics, and biological processes (Mazda et al., 2002; Rodríguez et al., 2017; Sandi et al., 2018; Willemsen et al., 2022). Globally, complex eco-hydrodynamic interactions govern how intertidal vegetation and landforms adapt to shifting sea levels, wave exposure, inundation frequencies, and salinity regimes (Cohen & Lara, 2003; Saintilan et al., 2018; Wimmler et al., 2021). Biological feedbacks also strongly modulate physical processes, for example, variations in canopy structure attenuate flow velocity and dissipate wave energy, while tidal inundation frequency directly dictates soil salinity within the root zone, thereby regulating plant growth, structural health, species competition, and spatial distribution (Dittmann et al., 2022; Wimmler et al., 2021).
While Figure 1.1 illustrates a canonical cross-section typical of hyper-arid coastal settings, where evapotranspiration generates an inverted landward hypersalinity gradient, similar intertidal habitat zonation occurs across tropical and subtropical coastlines worldwide (Cohen & Lara, 2003; Saintilan et al., 2018). However, the expression of these habitats varies substantially along climatic gradients because the balance between freshwater inputs and evaporative losses strongly influences salinity regimes and vegetation structure. In humid tropical environments, such as the Amazon Delta and Atlantic coast of South America, high river discharge and rainfall maintain relatively low root-zone salinities, supporting species-rich, high-biomass mangrove forests with canopy heights commonly exceeding \(20\text{-}30\ \mathrm{m}\) (Cohen & Lara, 2003; Reis et al., 2019). In contrast, arid and semi-arid coastlines experience limited rainfall, intense solar radiation, and high evaporative demand, conditions that favour salt accumulation in intertidal sediments. Climatic aridity can be characterised using the Aridity Index (AI), commonly defined as the ratio of mean annual precipitation (\(P\)) to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (\(PET\)):
\[
\mathrm{AI}=\frac{P}{PET}
\]
The index expresses the balance between water supplied by precipitation and the atmosphere’s potential demand for water through evapotranspiration. Lower AI values indicate increasingly arid conditions, in which precipitation is insufficient to meet potential evaporative demand; higher values indicate progressively more humid climates. Under a widely used classification, AI values below \(0.05\) indicate hyper-arid conditions, \(0.05\)–\(0.20\) indicate arid conditions, \(0.20\)–\(0.50\) indicate semi-arid conditions, and \(0.50\)–\(0.65\) indicate dry sub-humid conditions, with values above \(0.65\) generally representing humid climates (Adame et al., 2021; Zomer et al., 2022). Thus, an AI below \(0.20\) identifies arid climatic conditions in which persistent water deficits are likely, although local hydrological conditions may differ substantially where river discharge, groundwater inputs, tidal exchange, or episodic flooding provide additional water.
In intertidal environments, low AI values provide an indication of the climatic conditions that can promote hypersalinity, particularly in upper-intertidal flats where tidal flushing is infrequent and evaporation exceeds freshwater replenishment. Elevated sediment and porewater salinity can impose physiological stress on mangroves, contributing to reduced growth, canopy stature, productivity, and species diversity relative to humid tropical systems (Blanco-Sacristán et al., 2022). Nevertheless, AI is a regional climatic indicator rather than a direct measure of sediment salinity: actual salinity patterns also depend on tidal inundation, drainage, groundwater exchange, sediment properties, and local freshwater inputs. Consequently, the effects of aridity on mangrove distribution and structure must be interpreted in conjunction with site-specific hydrogeomorphic conditions.
Despite differences in climatic and hydrological conditions, arid and tropical intertidal environments commonly exhibit biological zonation associated with elevation, inundation frequency, salinity, and substrate conditions (Figure 1.1). Typical patterns include:
The spatial arrangement of these habitats varies geographically according to climate, tidal regime, geomorphology, and local hydrological conditions. In some tropical and humid subtropical systems, saltmarshes occur along the landward margins of mangrove forests, while in other settings they may extend towards the seaward margin or form mosaics with mangroves (Reis et al., 2019). In arid regions of Australia, mangroves commonly occupy lower intertidal creek margins, whereas saltmarshes, succulent samphire communities, and cyanobacterial mats may occupy higher and less frequently inundated areas (Saintilan et al., 2018). In some hyper-arid coastal environments, where saltmarsh vegetation is sparse or absent, mangroves may transition directly into unvegetated saline flats (Blanco-Sacristán et al., 2022; Cohen et al., 2020). These patterns highlight that intertidal zonation is not a universal sequence, but a spatial organisation shaped by the interaction of physical conditions and habitat-specific ecological tolerances.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Region
The Pilbara region in Western Australia is home to unique intertidal ecosystems, where extensive tidal creeks, salt flats, and low-lying coastal landforms create a complex eco-geomorphic setting. These arid-zone coastal wetlands are rare globally, as they are shaped by intricate interactions between salinity, sediment transport, and habitat zonation, which are in turn influenced by tidal cycles.






Figure 1.1: Sites of interest within the Pilbara region, showing the study locations at Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston.



Figure 1.1 shows the primary sites of interest within the Pilbara region: Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston. Across these sites, episodic inputs and flooding from the terrestrial edge interact dynamically with sea-level variability to create a complex inundation regime that redistributes salt, nutrients, and sediments across the intertidal landscape. However, despite the ecological significance of these environments, there remains limited data and significant gaps in our understanding of how different coastal units in this region behave, making it challenging for regulators and managers to assess the risks of coastal developments, guide conservation efforts, and respond to environmental change.
The intertidal areas of the West Pilbara Coast exhibit a distinct zonation of benthic coastal habitat (BCH) communities—transitioning from subtidal embayments to terrestrial margins across mangrove, samphire, and algal (cyanobacterial) mat environments. Broad salt-flat areas supporting algal mats experience an intricate ecohydrological regime governed by interactions between rainfall, evaporation, surface–groundwater exchange, and inundation frequencies driven by periodic tides and extreme events like tropical cyclones. These habitats likely provide substantial ecosystem subsidies to adjacent marine and terrestrial environments, yet the full extent of this support remains unknown.
Given the sensitivity of these BCH communities to altered inundation and salinity, abrupt shifts can easily trigger mortality and alter spatial distributions:






NoteKey Findings: Non-Linear Tipping Points



Case Study: Minor sea-level anomalies (on the order of 10 cm) during the 2015/16 El Niño event led to well-documented, widespread mangrove dieback across northern Australia (Lovelock et al., 2017). Furthermore, mangroves experiencing hypersalinity often have minimal adaptive capacity under severe stress, escalating tree mortality (Dittmann et al., 2022).


Complex physical and ecological feedbacks govern how vegetation and landforms adapt to shifting sea levels and salinity regimes (Sandi et al., 2018; Wimmler et al., 2021). Variations in vegetation canopy and structure alter flow attenuation (Rodríguez et al., 2017), while inundation patterns control root-zone soil salinity, impacting plant growth and persistence (Dittmann et al., 2022; Wimmler et al., 2021). By altering near-bed hydrodynamics, coastal vegetation strongly influences local sediment transport, erosion, and accretion, shaping long-term coastal landform evolution over years to decades. Consequently, vegetation health dictates a coastline’s capacity to buffer against hazards such as extreme storms and sea-level rise (Willemsen et al., 2022), as illustrated by historical mangrove losses in southern Asia that led directly to severe coastal erosion (Mazda et al., 2002).
The potential for intertidal habitat disruption stems primarily from local coastal developments and salt production operations superimposed onto broader climate change drivers (Guo et al., 2022), including sea-level rise, altered rainfall, shifting cyclone frequencies, and rising temperatures. While conceptual models (Eliot, 2013; Semeniuk, 1994) and localised site assessments exist, there remains a fundamental lack of baseline knowledge regarding the sensitivity of these habitats and their ecosystem services across the diverse landforms of the Pilbara Coast.
To address this gap, there is an urgent need to identify and quantify the potential effects of climate change and proposed salt farm infrastructure on the capacity of mangroves, samphire, and algal mats to adapt. Developing advanced conceptual and numerical models is essential for providing a holistic, predictive assessment of how these coupled ecological and morphological systems will respond to future environmental change.

title: 2  Controls on Coastal Ecosystems in Pilbara
text:
2.1 Intertidal Habitats of the Pilbara Region
The intertidal habitats of the Pilbara region are outlined in Chapter 1. In parts of the north-western Pilbara, particularly around Exmouth Gulf, the intertidal zone extends several kilometres landward, supporting a heterogeneous mosaic of mangroves, samphire and saltmarsh vegetation, cyanobacterial mats, salt flats, tidal creeks, and unvegetated sandy surfaces. The relative extent and spatial arrangement of these habitats vary with surface elevation, coastal morphology, and hydrological connectivity (Hickey et al., 2025).
Understanding the environmental controls on these habitats is important for interpreting their distribution and assessing how they may respond to future SLR. Water levels and salinity are two key controls on mangroves along with temperature for cyanobacterial mats, although their effects interact with substrate characteristics, sediment dynamics, and local geomorphology. For mangroves, elevation and hydroperiod (inundation frequency), duration, and depth of inundation strongly influence habitat distribution and persistence, while sediment accumulation and changes in surface elevation affect the capacity of mangrove environments to adjust to rising sea levels (Krauss et al., 2014; Woodroffe et al., 2016). Cyanobacterial mats in arid intertidal environments are also influenced by the balance between inundation and exposure, desiccation, and the exchange of water and dissolved materials with surrounding environments (Adame et al., 2012; Hickey et al., 2025; Lovelock et al., 2010).
Water levels in the Pilbara vary over several timescales. Astronomical tides produce regular inundation cycles, while seasonal and interannual variations in sea level alter the background water level on which these tides occur. These longer-term variations can be influenced by large-scale climate variability, including the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), which affects regional atmospheric and oceanographic conditions. Atmospheric pressure and wind forcing, particularly during extreme weather events, can generate additional water-level anomalies through storm surges and coastally trapped waves. Wind also influences coastal hydrodynamics by contributing to water-level setup and generating waves, with the magnitude of these effects depending on wind strength and direction, coastal exposure, and local bathymetry. Together, these processes influence the frequency, depth, and spatial extent of inundation across the region’s low-gradient intertidal flats.
Salinity is closely linked to the balance between evaporation, rainfall, tidal inundation, and drainage. Under the Pilbara’s arid climate, high temperatures and strong solar radiation promote evaporation, which can concentrate salts in surface water and sediment porewater during prolonged exposure. Rainfall can temporarily dilute these salts and provide freshwater inputs, while tidal exchange can introduce seawater and flush accumulated salts from inundated surfaces. Consequently, the salinity experienced by mangroves and cyanobacterial mats depends not only on climatic conditions but also on the frequency of marine inundation, local hydrological connectivity, and the duration of exposure between inundation events.
The following sections examine these controls in the context of the Pilbara region, beginning with observed water-level variability and its tidal, seasonal, interannual, and event-scale components. Regional weather and climate conditions are then considered alongside storm-driven water-level anomalies and wave processes. This provides the environmental context needed to understand the physical conditions that shape intertidal habitat distribution and may influence habitat responses to future environmental change.

text:
2.2 Sea level variability
Sea level variability is a dynamic phenomenon influenced by a range of oceanic, atmospheric, and geophysical processes operating across multiple temporal and spatial scales (Figure 2.1). These processes include short-term fluctuations such as tides, storm surges, and wave setup, as well as longer-term drivers such as seasonal variability, interannual climate oscillations, and long-term sea-level rise. The interaction of these processes results in complex patterns of water level variability that directly influence coastal environments.
Variations in sea level play a fundamental role in shaping coastal ecosystems by controlling the distribution and magnitude of hydrodynamic energy across the inner shelf and shoreline. Changes in water level alter wave transformation processes, influencing wave breaking, energy dissipation, and ultimately the exposure of coastal habitats to hydrodynamic forcing. This has direct implications for sediment transport pathways and the redistribution of sediments across coastal zones.
At the interface between marine and terrestrial systems such as beach-dune systems, tidal flats, and estuary-floodplain environments-sea level variability governs sediment dynamics by influencing erosion, deposition, and sediment exchange processes. Fluctuations in water levels determine the extent and duration of inundation, which in turn affects sediment resuspension, transport capacity, and the stability of geomorphic features.
In estuarine and shallow coastal environments, sea level variability is the primary driver of hydrological connectivity and water quality conditions. It regulates tidal exchange, salinity intrusion, and residence times, thereby influencing key ecological processes. For coastal ecosystems such as mangroves in the Pilbara region, sea level variability directly controls hydroperiod (frequency, duration, and depth of inundation), which is a critical determinant of mangrove distribution, productivity, and resilience.
Understanding sea level variability across different time scales is therefore essential for predicting the response of coastal ecosystems to environmental change, particularly in the context of accelerating sea-level rise and changing climate conditions.






Figure 2.1: Sea level variability as a function of time scales. Source: CSIRO.

2.3 Tides
Water levels in the Pilbara region are predominantly controlled by mixed, mainly semi-diurnal tides with meso- to macro-tidal ranges that increase from west to east. These tidal processes generate cyclical variations across multiple temporal scales, including fortnightly spring–neap cycles, biannual cycles driven by the Earth’s latitudinal tilt, 4.4-year cycles associated with lunar orbital variations, and the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle. While the 18.6-year modulation is pronounced in south-west Western Australia—altering tidal ranges by up to approximately 10 cm (20–30% of the mean tidal range)—its relative impact is less significant in the north-west (Eliot, 2012; Lowe et al., 2021). Nevertheless, even minor variations in tidal range strongly influence coastal processes and intertidal ecosystem dynamics.

title: 2  Controls on Coastal Ecosystems in Pilbara
text:
2.4 Seasonal and Interannual Variability
In addition to astronomical tides, water levels along the Western Australian coast vary seasonally and between years. Off the coast of Western Australia in the southeast Indian Ocean, regional surface circulation is dominated by the unique poleward-flowing, downwelling-favourable Leeuwin Current (Lowe et al., 2012). Large seasonal and interannual mean sea level variations are driven by steric effects (thermal expansion and contraction) and Ekman setup associated with alongshelf Leeuwin Current transport (Eliot, 2010). Non-tidal water level fluctuations contribute up to ~0.2 m in seasonal amplitude and ~0.3 m in interannual variance, superimposed onto astronomical tides.






Figure 2.2: Monthly mean water level variations (m AHD) from 2006 to 2022 at (a) Exmouth and (b) Onslow tide stations. Solid red lines represent the multi-year mean value, while individual colored lines denote individual years.



Figure 2.2 shows the measured monthly mean water level variations from 2006 to 2022 at the Exmouth (panel a) and Onslow (panel b) tide stations, plotted year-wise. Both locations exhibit a clear, synchronised seasonal signal: mean water levels peak during autumn (April–May) at values reaching up to ~0.25 to 0.30 m AHD on average (solid red line), driven by seasonal shifts in Leeuwin Current intensity, before falling to a seasonal minimum in late winter and early spring (August–September) at approximately 0.0 to 0.05 m AHD (Seashore Engineering, 2022).
In addition to this annual cycle, Figure 2.2 highlights substantial interannual variability across individual years (indicated by the spread of colored lines). The vertical variance band (up to ~0.4 m during early months like January and February) demonstrates how climate oscillations such as El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phases drive multi-year sea level variability above and below the baseline mean. Notably, Exmouth and Onslow track each other closely in terms of seasonal timing, multi-year means, and overall variance envelope, reflecting strong regional coherence across the West Pilbara Coast.

title: 2  Controls on Coastal Ecosystems in Pilbara
text:
2.5 Storm surge and coastally-trapped waves
Storm surge refers to deviations in mean sea level driven by atmospheric forcing, primarily associated with changes in barometric pressure and wind stress. These weather-induced fluctuations occur over time scales ranging from minutes to several days and can significantly elevate coastal water levels. The most substantial surges are typically generated by intense weather systems characterised by low atmospheric pressure and strong winds, and are therefore commonly referred to as storm surges.
In addition to locally generated surge, free surge responses can propagate beyond the region of direct atmospheric forcing. These include surface gravity waves, Kelvin waves, and coastally-trapped waves, which are generated by synoptic-scale systems and travel along the coastline (Trenberth, 1991). As these waves approach the coast, boundary constraints and decreasing water depth modify their behaviour. Shallowing conditions reduce propagation speeds and enhance water level responses, leading to the amplification of surge through shoaling processes. In semi-enclosed coastal environments, these boundary effects may also give rise to oscillatory motions such as seiches (Seashore Engineering, 2016).
Tropical cyclones are a major driver of extreme storm surge events in the Pilbara region. These systems are characterised by intense low-pressure centres and high wind speeds, with cyclone classification beginning at sustained winds of 63 km/h and reaching up to 276 km/h in extreme cases along the Western Australian coastline (Seashore Engineering, 2016). Tropical cyclones generate both large waves and significant storm surges, particularly as they approach and cross the coastline.
An important characteristic of cyclone-driven surge in this region is the role of coastally-trapped waves, which enable water level anomalies to propagate alongshore over large distances. As a result, cyclone-induced water level fluctuations can affect coastal areas far removed from the point of landfall. The magnitude and spatial distribution of surge are strongly influenced by cyclone track orientation. In the Pilbara, the highest surge events are typically associated with coast-crossing cyclones that generate strong onshore winds. Further west along the coast, however, extreme surge events are more commonly linked to cyclones travelling parallel to the coastline, which enhance the generation of coastally-trapped waves.
These processes are illustrated in Figure 2.3, which shows the tracks of tropical cyclones responsible for the highest observed surges along the Western Australian coast. Understanding the combined influence of atmospheric forcing, coastal geometry, and wave dynamics is critical for accurately assessing extreme water levels and their impacts on coastal ecosystems.






Figure 2.3: Tropical cyclone paths causing highest observed surges along the Western Australian coast (Seashore Engineering, 2016).

text:
2.6 Wave Climate

2.6.1 Ambient Wave Conditions
The hydrodynamic energy across the West Pilbara coast and Exmouth Gulf is overwhelmingly dominated by tidal and wind-driven processes, with ambient wave energy playing a minor, secondary role under normal conditions. Open ocean swell waves originating from the Southern Ocean and Indian Ocean are effectively blocked and sheltered by the landmass of the Exmouth.






Figure 2.4: Mean significant wave height (\(H_s\)) across the West Pilbara region derived from the Australian Climate Service Wave Hindcast (WHACS) dataset (1980–2023) (Smith et al., 2025). White contours denote mean \(H_s\) intervals (m), highlighting severe wave energy attenuation moving from deep offshore waters into sheltered embayments.



Figure 2.4 illustrates the long-term regional mean significant wave height (\(H_s\)) derived from the Wave Hindcast for Australian Coastal Seas (WHACS) dataset (1980–2023) (Smith et al., 2025). The spatial distribution clearly highlights the extreme wave energy gradients across the region:

Offshore and Western Margins: Moderate mean wave heights of 1.5 to >2.0 m persist in exposed deepwater areas west of the Exmouth Peninsula.
Sheltered Embayments and Nearshore Lands: As waves propagate past the peninsula into Exmouth Gulf and along the low-gradient inner shelf near Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston, depth-induced breaking and fetch constraints reduce mean significant wave heights to \(<0.5\) m (dark purple zone in Figure 2.4).

Ambient wave conditions within Exmouth Gulf and adjacent coastal flats are primarily locally generated wind-sea waves. Driven by seasonal wind regimes across the available fetches of the Gulf, these short-period ambient waves typically reach significant wave heights of less than 1.5 m. Consequently, regular, day-to-day ambient waves are not a dominant physical driver shaping the intertidal coastal landforms of this region.


2.6.2 Extreme Wave Conditions
While ambient wave energy is low, wave processes become highly significant during rare, extreme meteorological events. Long-term offshore waverider buoy deployments (2006–2012) recorded extreme wave events directly linked to severe tropical cyclones, such as TC Nicholas (February 2008), which generated offshore significant wave heights of 5.7 m with peak periods of 12 seconds (Seashore Engineering, 2022).
During severe tropical storms, extreme gale-force winds aligned with the north-facing mouth of Exmouth Gulf can drive substantial wave energy directly into the inner Gulf. Numerical modelling suggests cyclone-generated waves within the Gulf can reach 2.0–4.0 m significant height. However, the actual impact of extreme wave energy at inner-shelf locations (such as Giralia and Urala) is heavily modulated and attenuated by broad, shallow intertidal bathymetry and complex fringing reef/flat systems.

title: 2  Controls on Coastal Ecosystems in Pilbara
text:
2.7 Weather and climate variability
The Pilbara has an arid to semi-arid climate characterised by high temperatures, low and variable rainfall, and strong seasonal variation in wind conditions. Rainfall is episodic, with important contributions from tropical cyclones, convective storms and, in some coastal areas, winter weather systems. Temperature and rainfall influence the terrestrial water balance and evaporative demand, while winds influence coastal hydrodynamics through surface stress, local wave generation and, under suitable conditions, changes in coastal water levels (Charles et al., 2015; Seashore Engineering, 2022).

2.7.1 Rainfall
Mean annual rainfall across the Pilbara varies spatially, generally decreasing from the north towards the south. Regional climate assessments report annual totals of approximately 300–350 mm in parts of the north, declining to below 250 mm in some southern areas, while elevated inland areas such as the Hamersley Ranges can receive more than 500 mm annually Charles et al. (2015). Topography and the occurrence of convective and cyclonic systems contribute to this spatial variability.






Figure 2.5: Mean annual rainfall (mm/year) across the Assessment area for the period 1911–2012, highlighting the spatial gradient and elevated inland precipitation (Charles et al., 2015).



Rainfall near the coast is also strongly seasonal and variable between years. At Onslow, the monthly rainfall distribution shows contributions from early-summer rainfall events and, in some years, early-winter systems, separated by a comparatively dry period. The long-term monthly distribution and the 20th–80th percentile range are presented in Figure 2.6.






Figure 2.6: Monthly rainfall distribution at Onslow Airport (Station 5017) spanning 1911 to 2012, illustrating the mean monthly values and the 20th–80th percentile range (Charles et al., 2015).



The distribution illustrates (Figure 2.6) that rainfall is episodic rather than evenly distributed throughout the year. Consequently, monthly or annual averages do not fully represent the timing or duration of individual rainfall events. The timing of rainfall relative to tidal inundation and periods of surface exposure is particularly relevant when considering freshwater inputs and the salinity of intertidal surface water and sediment porewater.


2.7.2 Temperature
High temperatures and strong solar radiation characterise much of the Pilbara, particularly during the summer months. Regional climate data indicate that January is generally among the hottest months, although the timing of peak temperatures can vary between coastal and inland locations. Coastal sea breezes can moderate daytime temperatures relative to inland areas, while heat extremes remain an important feature of the regional climate (Charles et al., 2015) (Figure 2.7).






Figure 2.7: Monthly means of daily minimum (\(T_{min}\)), mean (\(T_{mean}\)), and maximum (\(T_{max}\)) temperatures across the Assessment area for the period 1911–2012 (Charles et al., 2015).



The regional temperature profile highlighted in Figure 2.7 is defined by the following characteristics:

Summer Maximums: Monthly mean daily maximums in January exceed 39°C across southwestern and eastern sectors, peaking at an average of 41°C at Marble Bar. Near-coastal sites near Onslow experience lower maximums due to sea-breeze moderation, though temperatures consistently exceed 35°C.
Extreme Records: Maximums above 45°C occur regularly between November and February. The state maximum temperature record of 50.5°C was recorded locally along the coast at Mardie on 19 February 1998.
Winter Minimums: July is the coldest month, with mean daily minimums ranging from 5–6°C in the south to 13–15°C along the northern coast. Sub-zero temperatures remain confined to inland southern areas (e.g., Nullagine recording -2.2°C).



2.7.3 Wind Regime
The baseline wind climate in the vicinity of Learmonth and the Onslow region transitions between seasonal trade wind systems and localised coastal circulations throughout the year.

Prevailing Direction: The region is anchored by a persistent southerly-to-southwesterly wind vector year-round. Across all 12 months, the dominant wind directions fall between 202.5° (SSW) and 225° (SW), which consistently record the highest directional frequencies in the dataset.
Spring to Late Summer Peak (October–March): As the inland heat low develops during warmer months, this southerly-to-southwesterly flow intensifies, reinforced by strong afternoon sea breezes. The dominance of 202.5° winds peaks sharply in October (37.2%) and November (36.3%), remaining exceptionally high through December (35.7%) and January (30.5%).
Winter Shift (May–August): During cooler months, the trade wind regime exerts a stronger influence, introducing a secondary peak from the easterly to southeasterly sector (135°–180°). From May through August, frequencies across 135°, 157.5°, and 180° increase significantly (e.g., 180° reaches 12.5%–13.1% in July–August), reflecting morning trade wind surges before shifting around to the south-southwest later in the day.
Transition Months (April & September): April and September represent transitional periods. April exhibits a broader spread across east, south, and south-southwest directions as summer sea breezes decline, while September marks the rapid re-establishment of the dominant south-southwesterly flow (31.7% at 202.5°).







Figure 2.8: Monthly directional distribution (%) of wind at Learmonth Station, displaying the seasonal evolution of prevailing south-southeasterly to south-southwesterly vectors.



As illustrated in Figure 2.8, while the overall wind regime is dominated by a year-round southerly-to-southwesterly corridor, the 12-month evolution is characterised by strong late-spring/summer amplification from coastal sea breezes and a secondary easterly trade component during winter.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
text:
3.1 Overview
To predict the spatial distribution, long-term persistence, and resilience of key intertidal habitats specifically mangrove forests and cyanobacterial (algal) mats it is essential to understand the primary physical and ecological drivers governing their dynamics. As established in Chapter 2, coastal ecosystem controls across the Pilbara region include complex interactions between hydrodynamics (water levels, flow velocities, and bed shear stress), salinity, surface temperature, light availability, microtopography, rainfall, and sedimentation rates. All of these factors interact to determine habitat suitability, colonisation boundaries, and ecological persistence.
Evaluating how these intertidal environments will respond over long-term (decadal-to-centennial) timescales under sea-level rise (SLR) requires robust predictive methodologies. Broadly, predictive approaches in coastal geomorphology and ecology fall into two main categories: observational/empirical methods (e.g., field monitoring, historical aerial photography, and satellite remote sensing) and numerical modelling frameworks.
Direct field measurements and satellite-derived remote sensing provide high-resolution spatial mapping of contemporary habitat extent and short-term baseline trends (Hickey et al., 2025). However, observational and empirical approaches alone cannot accurately project coastal ecosystem configurations 50 to 100 years into the future. Empirical extrapolations inherently assume that past environmental relationships will remain stationary. Under accelerating rates of SLR, coastal systems experience non-linear threshold behaviours, altered tidal prism dynamics, and unprecedented shifts in hydroperiod and sediment supply (Kirwan & Megonigal, 2013; Passeri et al., 2015). Furthermore, observational data cannot capture complex two-way eco-morphodynamic feedbacks—such as how shifting vegetation coverage continuously alters flow resistance, sediment trapping, and local bed elevation (Fagherazzi et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2022).
Consequently, numerical modelling provides a means of investigating the long-term responses of intertidal habitats to sea-level rise and other environmental changes. Hydrodynamic and morphodynamic models resolve the physical processes governing water movement, sediment transport and changes in bed elevation, while ecological models represent vegetation dynamics and their responses to environmental conditions (Kernkamp et al., 2011; Lesser et al., 2004; Piercy et al., 2024). Integrating these processes can help investigate feedbacks between hydrodynamics, sediment dynamics and habitat development, and assess potential responses to future climate change and coastal development scenarios beyond those represented in historical observations. However, the extent to which these interactions are captured depends on the processes included in the model, and comprehensive ecological and physical modelling remains computationally and methodologically challenging (Fanous et al., 2023; Piercy et al., 2024; Woodroffe et al., 2016).
When evaluating long-term ecosystem responses to SLR through numerical models, accounting for morphodynamic adjustments becomes critical. Long-term changes in inundation duration and depth are not solely dictated by the rate of SLR, but also depend on intertidal topography and eco-morphological feedbacks, which are in turn governed by hydro-sedimentary boundary forcings including tidal range, wave action, and sediment supply (FitzGerald et al., 2008; Passeri et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2022). Mangrove forests and algal mats can only tolerate specific durations and frequencies of tidal submersion (Woodroffe et al., 2016). Because hydrodynamic shifts under SLR continuously reshape intertidal morphodynamics, these physical (relevant forcings) and biological processes must be modelled in a dynamically coupled, two-way manner.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
section: 3.2 Advances and Limitations in Eco-Geomorphic Modelling
text:
3.2 Advances and Limitations in Eco-Geomorphic Modelling
To bridge the gap between physical and ecological processes, hybrid and coupled eco-geomorphic (bio-hydro-morphodynamic) frameworks have been developed to simulate vegetation expansion, retreat, and decadal eco-geomorphic evolution (Fagherazzi et al., 2012; Lesser et al., 2004). Notable examples include:

Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM) coupled with the MesoFON individual-based mangrove model (DFMFON) (Beselly et al., 2023; Kernkamp et al., 2011).
DFM integrated with custom MATLAB or Python vegetation modules (Willemsen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022).
The BASEMENT hydro-eco-morphodynamic model coupled with the Python-based BASEveg vegetation module (Caponi et al., 2023).

Despite their ability to capture multi-way feedbacks between biological dynamics and hydro-morphology, existing coupled frameworks suffer from severe computational bottlenecks. Because they must resolve non-linear interactions across vast spatial and temporal scales, previous applications have been restricted either to idealised domains (Willemsen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022) or relatively small localized estuaries (Beselly et al., 2023). A scalable, process-based approach capable of modelling complex coastal systems and regional-scale domains has been unavailable.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
text:
3.3 Predictive Approaches for Target Habitats

3.3.1 Mangrove Eco-Geomorphology
Mangrove forests occupy the mid-to-upper intertidal zone and rely on a precise balance between inundation frequency, bed shear stress, sediment supply, and salinity. Within the coupled framework, mangrove dynamics are represented via process-based two-way feedbacks: DFM simulates the local hydrodynamic stress and bed level changes, while updated canopy density and root structures alter hydraulic roughness and attenuate wave and current energy. Due to numerical stability constraints, we did not include salinity in our coupled mangrove model.


3.3.2 Cyanobacterial (Algal) Mat Dynamics
Algal mats develop on supratidal and upper intertidal land surfaces subject to periodic inundation and local ponding, particularly salt flats, mudflats, and overbank basins adjoining tidal creeks (Seashore Engineering, 2021, 2022; Taukulis et al., 2018). The ecological drivers regulating algal mat establishment, growth, and survival include hydroperiod (inundation duration and frequency), salinity, surface elevation, ambient temperature, light, sedimentation, and hydrodynamic bed stress.
In the semi-arid Pilbara region, the upper intertidal zone is exceptionally flat and only occasionally inundated. Microtopography (such as swash lines, low-relief sediment ridges, and sparse vegetation) causes localised ponding, where high evaporation rates generate hypersaline conditions favoured by opportunistic, nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria (Seashore Engineering, 2021; Taukulis et al., 2018). Thick mats bind surface sediments, reduce bed permeability, and alter local drainage pathways.
Currently, no dedicated process-based numerical tools exist to simulate dynamic algal mat growth, colonisation, or two-way morphodynamic feedbacks. Existing predictions regarding the response of upper intertidal flats to sea-level rise do not explicitly account for biological algal mat interactions, but instead evaluate predicted changes to tidal flow distributions and disturbance regimes (Seashore Engineering, 2021; Townend et al., 2011).
Prior habitat prediction efforts relied primarily on static hydroperiod approaches—relating mapped mat distributions directly to tidal elevation contours and projecting linear upward shifts under SLR (Seashore Engineering, 2021). Under standard Pilbara conditions, both the upper limit (constrained by desiccation) and the lower limit (constrained by bioturbation and excessive inundation) shift landward with rising sea levels. However, local features such as low-relief sediment ridges alter hydroperiod dynamics, creating local non-linear responses that simple elevation-based projections cannot capture.
To address this limitation, our approach utilises the calibrated DFM hydro-morphodynamic model (which incorporates two-way mangrove-morphodynamic updates) to explicitly model future hydrodynamic and hydroperiod conditions suitable for algal mat survival. The hydrodynamic parameters governing inundation patterns and shear stresses are calibrated against present-day baseline conditions, using satellite-derived spatial mapping of observed algal mat locations (Hickey et al., 2025). The hydrodynamic model outputs are then evaluated against critical hydroperiod thresholds to predict potential areas of future algal mat colonisation, migration, or loss under SLR scenarios.

title: 3  Approach: Dynamic Modelling Framework
text:
3.3 The Dynamically Coupled Bio-Hydro-Morphodynamic Framework
Delft3D Flexible Mesh was selected as the core hydrodynamic–morphodynamic model for this study as it is an established, open-source (for academic) modelling platform for simulating coastal hydrodynamics, sediment transport and morphological evolution (Kernkamp et al., 2011). DFM has also been adopted in several studies coupling vegetation dynamics with hydrodynamic and morphological processes, including the frameworks developed by Xie et al. (2022); Willemsen et al. (2022); Beselly et al. (2023); Dunlop et al. (2025). These developments provided a methodological basis for selecting DFM as the physical modelling component of the framework developed here.
Building on this approach, we developed a dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic modelling framework integrating DFM with a vegetation module based on NBSDynamics (Nature-Based Solutions Dynamics) (Deltares, 2022), incorporating ecological parameterisation strategies adapted from Xie et al. (2022), Berger & Hildenbrandt (2000) and Van Maanen et al. (2015). A custom Python coupling interface manages information exchange between the hydro-morphodynamic model and the vegetation module, enabling the framework to run on high-performance computing (HPC) clusters and support spatially extensive simulations.

3.3.1 Model integration and information exchange
As illustrated in Figure 3.1, the framework represents interactions between hydrodynamic conditions, vegetation dynamics and morphological evolution through a two-way coupling process. DFM resolves hydrodynamics and sediment transport, while the vegetation module evaluates mangrove establishment, growth and mortality in response to environmental conditions. The resulting changes in vegetation properties are then returned to DFM to update spatially varying flow resistance and bed roughness.
The coupling operates through the following sequence at defined coupling intervals:

Hydrodynamic and morphodynamic simulation: DFM concurrently simulates hydrodynamics and sediment transport, calculating spatially distributed water levels, flow velocities, bed shear stresses, and bed level changes across the intertidal domain. These variables define the physical and morphological environment experienced by the vegetation.
Environmental output transfer: The Python coupling interface extracts and transfers the integrated hydrodynamic and morphodynamic outputs (water levels, bed shear stresses, and updated bed elevations) to the vegetation module.
Vegetation response and updates: At designated vegetation time steps, the vegetation module evaluates mangrove colonisation, growth, and mortality based on the updated environmental conditions and ecological thresholds. It then updates spatially distributed vegetation properties, including stem height, stem diameter, and stem density.
Feedback to hydro-morphodynamics: Updated vegetation parameters are converted into spatially varying flow resistance and drag parameters within DFM. This allows the evolving canopy and root structures to alter flow patterns and sediment transport in subsequent coupling steps.

This iterative exchange enables the framework to represent feedbacks between hydrodynamics, sediment transport, morphological evolution and mangrove development. Rather than prescribing vegetation as a static source of flow resistance, the framework allows vegetation properties and the physical environment to evolve in response to one another.
Unlike the mangrove component, cyanobacterial mats are represented using a decoupled, data-driven habitat-suitability approach. Although developing a mechanistic model of cyanobacterial mat dynamics coupled to hydrodynamics and sediment transport is technically feasible, such an approach would require substantial development, calibration and validation. In particular, reliable numerical representation of mat dynamics requires a more comprehensive understanding of their responses to environmental forcing, including light availability, temperature, salinity and hydrodynamic conditions, as well as sufficient observational data to parameterise and validate these relationships. Developing and validating such a model would extend beyond the timeframe of this project.
We therefore adopted a data-driven approach Chapter 20 that uses the outcomes of the mangrove modelling framework to inform the hydrodynamic simulations from which potential cyanobacterial mat habitats are assessed. Specifically, the mangrove predictions provide the evolving vegetation distribution used to update the hydrodynamic representation, while cyanobacterial mat suitability is evaluated separately using the resulting hydrodynamic conditions. Eco-hydrodynamic thresholds derived from present-day satellite-based mat distributions are then used to identify areas with physical conditions consistent with observed mat habitats (Hickey et al., 2025). This approach enables the potential redistribution of cyanobacterial mats to be assessed under changing physical conditions without explicitly simulating microbial growth, mat biomass or mat-driven morphological feedbacks. The data-driven method and its implementation are described in Section 4.5.






Figure 3.1: Schematic representation of the dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic modelling framework. Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM) simulates hydrodynamics, sediment transport and morphological change, while the vegetation module represents mangrove colonisation, growth and mortality. A Python coupling interface exchanges physical forcing and updated vegetation properties between the two components. Cyanobacterial mat suitability is assessed separately using hydrodynamic outputs.





3.3.2 Accelerating long-term simulations
The primary objective of the framework is to investigate intertidal habitat changes over centennial timescales across coastal-scale domains. Explicitly simulating every hydrodynamic and morphodynamic process over hundreds of years, while repeatedly updating vegetation, would impose substantial computational demands. We therefore employed the morphological acceleration factor (\(f_{\mathrm{mor}}\)) in DFM to accelerate bed-level evolution relative to the simulated hydrodynamic time.
A morphological acceleration factor of \(f_{\mathrm{mor}} = 50\) was adopted, such that approximately two years of hydrodynamic simulation could represent 100 years of morphological evolution under the accelerated-morphology assumption. This approach reduces the computational burden of long-term simulations while retaining spatially explicit hydrodynamic and sediment-transport calculations. Existing studies have also employed a similar morphological acceleration in coupled vegetation and morphodynamic studies, including those by Willemsen et al. (2022); Xie et al. (2022); Beselly et al. (2023); Dunlop et al. (2025).
However, accelerating morphological evolution does not automatically ensure that ecological processes remain consistent with the accelerated simulation timescale. Vegetation growth, establishment and mortality must be treated consistently with the temporal scaling applied to the physical processes; otherwise, the relative rates of vegetation development and morphological adjustment may become unrealistic. The coupling configuration and temporal treatment of the model components are described in more detail in Chapter 4.
Morphological acceleration also has implications for the interpretation of environmental forcing. In particular, transient water-level events, such as storm surges, should not necessarily be treated as representative of the long-term conditions experienced over the accelerated morphological timescale. The selection of hydrodynamic forcing therefore required consideration of the dominant tidal constituents and the broader water-level variability characteristic of the West Pilbara coast.


3.3.3 Derivation of representative tidal forcing
As discussed in Chapter 2, the West Pilbara coast experiences substantial water-level variability arising from astronomical tides, seasonal and interannual fluctuations, tropical cyclones and other meteorological processes. These variations influence inundation frequency and duration, sediment transport and the environmental conditions experienced by intertidal vegetation. Although such variability can affect long-term habitat trajectories, directly imposing the complete observed water-level record within a morphologically accelerated simulation may disproportionately amplify transient events relative to the timescale of morphological evolution.
To establish a representative tidal forcing for the long-term simulations, we therefore performed harmonic analysis of water-level observations from the Exmouth and Onslow tide gauges. The analysis was conducted using the Python implementation of UTide (Codiga, 2011), which estimates the amplitudes and phases of astronomical tidal constituents from observed water-level time series. The extracted constituents were ranked according to their contribution to the reconstructed tidal signal, and the four dominant constituents were selected to represent the principal tidal variability.
The four selected constituents were M2, S2, K1, and O1. Together, these account for approximately over 90% of the reported tidal energy across both analysis sites. Their frequencies, amplitudes, phases, and percentage energy contributions are summarised in Table 3.1.

The analysis of both tide gauges provided a basis for characterising the tidal regime across the study region. For simplicity, however, a single representative water-level forcing was applied across all study sites, as described in Table 3.1 and Section 1.4. This provides a consistent basis for comparing habitat responses between sites, although it does not capture all local differences in tidal amplitude, phase and water-level variability.
It it important to highlight that the use of the four dominant constituents also represents a deliberate simplification of the observed water-level regime. Seasonal and interannual variability, including variations associated with the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), can influence inundation patterns and sediment dynamics. The duration and timing of these variations may affect vegetation establishment, mortality and morphological adjustment, potentially producing different habitat trajectories even under the same long-term mean sea-level trend. The selected harmonic constituents do not explicitly reproduce these seasonal, interannual or event-driven variations.
Nevertheless, the purpose of the representative forcing is to establish a consistent baseline for investigating long-term habitat changes under the principal astronomical tidal controls, rather than to reproduce every short-term fluctuation in observed water levels. The resulting predictions should therefore be interpreted in the context of this forcing assumption, with the potential influence of omitted seasonal, interannual and extreme-event variability recognised as a source of uncertainty.


3.3.4 Salinity representation and model limitations
Salinity is an important environmental control on mangrove establishment, growth and survival, particularly in the hyper-arid West Pilbara, where evaporation, limited freshwater input and restricted tidal exchange can produce hypersaline conditions. Field observations indicate that salinity is approximately 35–55 ppt near creek mouths, increases towards the landward intertidal zone and can exceed 140 ppt across salt-flat environments. These spatial gradients suggest that salinity may constrain mangrove colonisation even where inundation and elevation conditions become physically suitable.
During initial sensitivity testing, we encountered two difficulties when attempting to represent salinity in the modelling framework. First, stable simulations (short term runs) did not reproduce the high salinity concentrations observed in the landward intertidal and salt-flat environments, with modelled values generally remaining below approximately 55 ppt. Second, longer simulations exhibited numerical instability associated with wetting and drying transitions. In some runs, salinity increased sharply in cells undergoing wetting and drying, eventually reaching the model’s upper limit of 500 ppt. These extreme values (instability) subsequently spread across the computational domain, causing the simulation to crash.
These behaviours may be associated with the numerical treatment of salt during wetting and drying, including the handling of accumulated salt as cells become dry. However, the underlying cause was not investigated further, and the observed instability cannot be attributed conclusively to a particular numerical mechanism.
Consequently, salinity was excluded from the predictive framework. However, it is possible to indirectly represent the influence of salinity through other variables, such as the timing and duration of inundation events, the inundation fittness curve of the mangrove growth (see also ?sec-urala-mangrove where we attempt to include the influence). It is noteworthy to mention that several existing studies have also omitted salinity in their approach e.g., Xie et al. (2022); Van Maanen et al. (2015); Willemsen et al. (2022); Dunlop et al. (2025). The omission reflects a modelling constraint rather than an assumption that salinity is ecologically unimportant.
This simplification has important implications for interpreting the predictions. Even with the indirect representation of salinity, the framework can identify locations where the modelled physical conditions are consistent with mangrove establishment, but it cannot independently determine whether salinity would permit successful establishment or sustained growth. Consequently, some locations predicted to be suitable may remain unsuitable under actual hypersaline conditions, particularly in the upper intertidal zone and on salt flats. The resulting predictions should therefore be interpreted as potential habitat distributions under the represented physical and ecological processes, rather than definitive forecasts of realised mangrove distribution.

title: 4  Model Overview
4  Model Overview
4  Model Overview
text:
4.3 Morphodynamic Module
Sediment transport and morphological evolution are simulated using the Delft3D-FM morphodynamic module (D-Morphology). Suspended sediment transport is calculated using the advection–diffusion equation:
\[
\frac{\partial c}{\partial t}
+
\frac{\partial (uc)}{\partial x}
+
\frac{\partial (vc)}{\partial y}
+
\frac{\partial ((w-w_s)c)}{\partial z}
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}
\left(
\epsilon_{s,x}
\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}
\right)
+
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
\left(
\epsilon_{s,y}
\frac{\partial c}{\partial y}
\right)
+
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}
\left(
\epsilon_{s,z}
\frac{\partial c}{\partial z}
\right)
\tag{4.13}\]
where \(c\) is the sediment concentration, \(u\), \(v\), and \(w\) are the flow velocity components in the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) directions, respectively, \(w_s\) is the sediment settling velocity, and \(\epsilon_{s,x}\), \(\epsilon_{s,y}\), and \(\epsilon_{s,z}\) are sediment diffusivities in each spatial direction.
For the present depth-averaged (2DH) model configuration, vertical transport terms are neglected. Boundary conditions at the free surface and bed define the exchange of suspended sediment between the water column and the seabed. At the free surface, the vertical diffusive flux is assumed to be zero:
\[
-w_s c - \varepsilon_{s,z}\frac{\partial c}{\partial z}=0,
\qquad
\text{at } z=\zeta \; (\text{free surface})
\tag{4.14}\]
The exchange of sediment between the bed and the water column is represented through erosion and deposition fluxes. The bed boundary condition is expressed as:
\[
-w_s c-\varepsilon_{s,z}\frac{\partial c}{\partial z}
=
D-E,
\qquad
\text{at } z=z_b \; (\text{bed level})
\tag{4.15}\]
where \(E\) and \(D\) represent the erosion and deposition fluxes, respectively. For cohesive sediments, erosion and deposition are calculated using the Partheniades–Krone formulations (Partheniades, 1965):
\[
E=
\begin{cases}
M
\left(
\frac{\tau_{b,\max}}{\tau_{cr,e}}-1
\right),
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}>\tau_{cr,e},
\\[8pt]
0,
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}\leq\tau_{cr,e},
\end{cases}
\tag{4.16}\]
\[
D=
\begin{cases}
w_s c
\left(
1-\frac{\tau_{b,\max}}{\tau_{cr,d}}
\right),
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}<\tau_{cr,d},
\\[8pt]
0,
&
\text{when }
\tau_{b,\max}\geq\tau_{cr,d}.
\end{cases}
\tag{4.17}\]
where \(M\) is the erosion parameter, \(\tau_{b,\max}\) is the maximum bed shear stress generated by currents and waves, \(\tau_{cr,e}\) is the critical bed shear stress for erosion, \(\tau_{cr,d}\) is the critical bed shear stress for deposition, \(w_s\) is the sediment settling velocity, and \(c\) is the depth-averaged suspended sediment concentration.

The coupled hydrodynamic, wave, and morphodynamic processes provide the physical framework required to simulate coastal ecosystem development, including feedbacks between vegetation establishment, flow modification, sediment dynamics, and morphological change.
Overall, the Delft3D-FM framework enables an integrated simulation of hydrodynamics, waves, sediment transport, and vegetation feedbacks, providing a robust tool for assessing coastal ecosystem dynamics under varying environmental conditions.

title: 4  Model Overview
text:
4.4 Mangrove Model

4.4.1 Colonisation
Mangrove establishment, growth, and mortality were explicitly coupled to local hydrodynamics through an inundation suitability framework. Colonisation is controlled jointly by inundation frequency (\(P\)) and hydrodynamic bed shear stress (\(\tau_{90}\)). These are optimised for each site specifically, however, for illustrative purposes, thresholds optimised for Giralia site is shown below.
Establishment can only occur within a bounded inundation window (\(P_{\min} \le P \le P_{\max}\), where \(P_{\min} = 0.05\) and \(P_{\max} = 0.60\)). Outside this range, establishment is not permitted, reflecting physiological limits on mangrove tolerance to submergence and desiccation. Within this window, colonisation is further constrained by bed shear stress:
\[
\tau_{90} \le \tau_{\text{thres}} \quad \text{where} \quad \tau_{\text{thres}} = 0.265 \text{ N m}^{-2}
\]
This adopted shear stress threshold falls within typical ranges reported in literature (Beselly et al., 2023; Willemsen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022). Within this feasible hydrodynamic domain, the probability of establishment is directly proportional to an inundation suitability function, \(I(P)\). When shear stress exceeds the threshold (\(\tau_{90} > \tau_{\text{thres}}\)), colonisation is completely inhibited regardless of inundation suitability.


4.4.2 Inundation Suitability Framework
Similar to existing formulations (Berger & Hildenbrandt, 2000; Van Maanen et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2022), the inundation suitability function \(I(P)\) is defined as a quadratic response to inundation frequency \(P\):
\[
I(P) = \max \left( a_s P^2 + b_s P + c_s,\, 0 \right)
\tag{4.18}\]
where \(a_s = -13.22\), \(b_s = 8.59\), and \(c_s = -0.40\). The parameters \(a_s\), \(b_s\), \(c_s\), as well as \(\tau_{\text{thres}}\) and the inundation range, were optimised by conducting sensitivity simulations against LiDAR-derived vegetation boundaries and hydrodynamics simulated for the calibration period (January–December 2024).
This formulation yields a unimodal response with a maximum suitability (\(I(P) \approx 1.0\)) at intermediate inundation frequencies.


4.4.3 Vegetation Growth
Vegetation growth is modelled as a stem diameter increment rate \(\frac{dD}{dt}\), scaled jointly by inundation suitability \(I(P)\) and a space availability factor \(C_f\) (adapted from Xie et al., 2022):
\[
\frac{dD}{dt} = \frac{G \cdot D \left( 1 - \frac{D \cdot H}{D_{\max} \cdot H_{\max}} \right)}{274 + 3 b_2 D - 4 b_3 D^2} \cdot I(P) \cdot C_f
\tag{4.19}\]
where \(G = 4.39\) is a growth coefficient, \(D\) is stem diameter (\(\text{cm}\)), and tree height \(H\) (\(\text{cm}\)) is expressed as:
\[
H = 137 + b_2 D - b_3 D^2
\]
with growth coefficients \(b_2 = 21.3\) and \(b_3 = 0.2\). The maximum structural dimensions (\(D_{\max} = 10 \text{ cm}\) and \(H_{\max} = 330 \text{ cm}\)) were established based on field observations and radiocarbon-dated chronology of arid Western Australian mangroves (Santini et al., 2013), while \(H_{\max}\) was further cross-referenced with regional \(98^{\text{th}}\) percentile LiDAR canopy height measurements. Growth parameters (\(G, b_2, b_3\)) were adjusted following Xie et al. (2022) to reflect growth responses under arid environmental conditions.
Growth is optimised within intermediate inundation frequencies where \(I(P)\) peaks. As trees approach maximum structural limits (\(D \to D_{\max}\)), the growth rate asymptotically approaches zero, representing the reduced growth increment characteristic of mature individuals.


4.4.4 Biomass and Spatial Footprint
To model cohort growth and evaluate total stand biomass within each grid cell, allometric relations based on stem diameter \(D\) (\(\text{m}\)) were implemented following Xie et al. (2022). Total standing biomass \(B_{\text{total}}\) (\(\text{kg}\)) per grid cell is calculated by summing aboveground and belowground biomass across all \(N\) cohorts present:
\[
B_{\text{total}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} n_i \left( \alpha_1 D_i^{\beta_1} + \alpha_2 D_i^{\beta_2} \right)
\tag{4.20}\]
where \(n_i\) and \(D_i\) are the stem density and stem diameter of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) cohort, respectively. Parameters \(\alpha_1, \beta_1\) represent aboveground biomass scaling, and \(\alpha_2, \beta_2\) represent belowground biomass scaling (Xie et al., 2022).
To quantify resource competition thresholds, a critical uncompeted stand capacity \(B_{\text{cap}}\) (\(\text{kg}\)) was derived using a “zone of influence” approach. This describes a fully stocked grid cell occupied by uninhibited mature mangroves (\(D = D_{\max}\)). The territorial footprint radius \(R_{\text{zoi}}\) (\(\text{m}\)) for a mature tree is defined as:
\[
R_{\text{zoi}} = 100 \cdot \left(\frac{D_{\max}}{2}\right)
\tag{4.21}\]
where \(100\) scales the stem radius to its zone of influence footprint. Assuming each mature tree occupies a square spatial footprint of side length \(2 R_{\text{zoi}}\), the maximum uncompeted biomass capacity for a cell area \(A_{\text{cell}}\) (\(\text{m}^2\)) is:
\[
B_{\text{cap}} = \left( \frac{A_{\text{cell}}}{(2 R_{\text{zoi}})^2} \right) \cdot B_{\text{single}}
\tag{4.22}\]
where \(B_{\text{single}}\) is the total individual biomass of a single mature tree (\(D = D_{\max}\)). \(B_{\text{cap}}\) serves as the baseline threshold for evaluating growth suppression and density-dependent mortality.


4.4.5 Intraspecific Competition
To account for spatial limits and resource constraints (e.g. light, space, and porewater nutrients) as vegetation matures, intraspecific competition is governed by a sigmoidal space/resource availability factor (\(C_f \in [0, 1]\)). It is computed as a function of total standing biomass \(B_{\text{total}}\):
\[
C_f = \frac{1}{1 + e^{d \cdot (B_{\text{total}} - B_{0.5})}}
\tag{4.23}\]
where \(B_{0.5}\) is the half-saturation biomass threshold at which resource stress reduces space availability to \(50\%\) (\(C_f = 0.5\)), and \(d\) is a scaling parameter controlling response steepness. Under low biomass conditions (\(B_{\text{total}} \ll B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f \to 1\), imposing negligible competitive inhibition. As biomass increases towards canopy closure (\(B_{\text{total}} \gg B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f \to 0\), representing maximal suppression.
Combined multi-factor environmental stress is evaluated as the product of inundation suitability and space availability (\(I(P) \cdot C_f\)). Intense competitive stress (\(C_f \to 0\)) depresses overall viability, slowing growth rates and initiating density-dependent self-thinning.


4.4.6 Mortality and Density Regulation
Vegetation mortality and density regulation follow a multi-factor, two-stage process driven by hydrodynamic stress, density-dependent competition, and desiccation. Total environmental stress is tracked via the combined viability product \(I(P) \cdot C_f\).
Sub-optimal conditions occur when total viability falls below a critical threshold (\(I(P) \cdot C_f < S_{\text{crit}}\)). For cells experiencing sub-optimal viability, a persistent stress counter \(T_{\text{stress}}\) is incremented sequentially at each time step; otherwise, \(T_{\text{stress}}\) resets to zero.

Complete Mortality: Triggered when a cell experiences sustained stress for five consecutive time steps (\(T_{\text{stress}} \ge 5\)) while simultaneously falling below a critical inundation threshold (\(I(P) < I_{\text{crit}}\)). Upon complete mortality, all structural vegetation attributes—stem density, stem diameter, canopy height, and root density—are reset to zero. Mature individuals are assumed to possess a maximum of \(1,000\) roots, with root counts updated following Van Maanen et al. (2015).
Self-Thinning: In cells subjected to stress (\(I(P) \cdot C_f < S_{\text{crit}}\)) that do not meet the full mortality criteria, self-thinning is applied by incrementally reducing stem density \(n_i\) by a fixed mortality rate factor \(m_{\text{rate}}\). Following self-thinning, \(B_{\text{total}}\) and \(C_f\) are dynamically re-evaluated to reflect the updated stand density.

Under low biomass conditions (\(B_{\text{total}} \ll B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f\) approaches zero, imposing negligible competitive limitations. As canopy closure and root crowding progress (\(B_{\text{total}} \gg B_{0.5}\)), \(C_f\) asymptotically approaches unity, reflecting maximum competition (acting as a proxy for light, space, and porewater nutrients). This competition factor directly modulates individual tree growth rates and exacerbates baseline environmental stress in densely populated grid cells.


4.4.7 Mortality and Self-Thinning
Vegetation mortality and density regulation were executed as a multi-factor, two-stage process influenced by hydrodynamic stress, density-dependent competition, and desiccation. Total environmental stress was computed as the joint product of inundation suitability (\(I(P)\)) and competition stress (\(C_f\)). Sub-optimal conditions were identified wherever total stress fell below a critical threshold:
\[
I(P) \times C_f \le 0.45
\]
For all grid cells outside suitable conditions, a persistent stress counter (\(\text{Mort}\)) was incremented sequentially; otherwise, the counter was reset to zero.

Complete Mortality: Triggered when a cell experiences sustained stress for five consecutive time steps (\(\text{Mort} \ge 5\), equivalent to 5 morphodynamic years) while simultaneously remaining below the critical threshold (\(I(P) \times C_f \le 0.45\)). Upon complete mortality, all structural vegetation attributes—including stem density, stem diameter, canopy height, and root density—were reset to zero.
Self-Thinning: In grid cells subjected to stress (\(I(P) \times C_f \le 0.45\)) that did not fulfill the complete mortality duration criteria, self-thinning was applied by incrementally reducing plant stem density by a fixed mortality rate factor (\(\text{Mort}_{\text{plant}}\)), after which \(C_f\) was dynamically re-evaluated to reflect the updated biomass density.

Similar to existing work (Xie et al., 2022), we assume a mature mangrove can have at most 1,000 roots. The number of roots is calculated following the approach of Van Maanen et al. (2015).

title: 5  Idealised Hydromorphological modelling
text:
5.1 Introduction
Intertidal flats form the transition between the ocean and the land and are periodically exposed between the lowest and highest astronomical tides. Their morphology is shaped by interactions among coastal hydrodynamics, sedimentary processes, and biological activity. The morphological evolution of tidal flats can be characterised in terms of profile shape, bed slope, and sediment properties, which vary systematically with sediment supply, wave conditions, and tidal forcing (Friedrichs, 2011). When averaged over annual or longer timescales, tidal-flat morphology may approach a state of dynamic equilibrium with the prevailing external forcing. For example, tide-dominated environments generally favour convex-upward tidal-flat profiles, whereas wave-dominated environments tend to produce concave profiles (Friedrichs & Perry, 2001).
The Pilbara coast of Western Australia is characterised by considerable spatial variability in tidal forcing, bed profiles, sediment composition, and sediment availability. To support the development and interpretation of regional morphodynamic models for sites along the Pilbara coast, including Giralia, Urala, and Cape Preston, it is necessary to understand how tidal-flat morphology responds to these environmental drivers.
Understanding this morphological response is a crucial factor that requires careful model calibration. However, spatially varying sediment-related information along the region remains limited, despite the availability of localised point data at Giralia and Urala. Calibrating the morphodynamic model is therefore essential to ensure that simulated morphological responses to future sea-level rise can be trusted. To determine and justify these morphodynamic parameters on sound physical grounds, this study resorts to idealised modelling. Specifically, this chapter uses schematised bathymetry and tidal forcing to systematically investigate the morphological responses of tidal flats under different environmental conditions.

title: 5  Idealised Hydromorphological modelling
text:
5.2 Model settings
The exploratory model was run by Delft3D Flexible Mesh, using the D-Flow and D-Morphology module to simulate hydrodynamics and sediment transport. The model was run in a two-dimensional (depth-averaged) domain \(2\times 20\ \mathrm{km}\) with an offshore open boundary, using a rectangular grid size of \(50 \times 50\ \mathrm{m}\). The offshore open boundary was driven by tidal constituents, e.g. M2 and M4, and the lateral and offshore boundaries were closed to ensure model stability. The model bathymetry was featured by alongshore uniform slope of 0.07%. An further mild slope of 0.035% on the high intertidal flat was applied to the model for initial bed profile sensitivity test. The initial bed level at the open boundary was set to-7m relative to mean sea level (MSL) to ensure that cross-shore tidal movement would not be obstructed by the landward boundary. Random perturbations of \(5\ \mathrm{cm}\) were superimposed on the bathymetry to initiate simulations.
Both sand and mud were considered in the idealised model. Sand transport followed the formulation of (Rijn, 1993), with the median grain size of 0.25mm. Mud transport was computed using the Partheniades’ equation (Sanford & Halka, 1993; Winterwerp J.C., 2007), with settling velocity of 0.25 mm/s and critical erosion shear stress of 0.1Pa. Bed friction was represented by a uniform Manning’s friction coefficient of 0.023 \(s\ m^{-1/3}\) . A constant mud supply was imposed at the open boundary. To accelerate morphological response to hydrodynamics, a morphological accelerator Morfac of 50 was used in this model.






Figure 5.1: Idealised model domain and cross section profile

title: 5  Idealised Hydromorphological modelling
text:
5.3 Scenarios design
The scenarios were designed to investigate morphological responses to variations in tidal range, tidal asymmetry, initial bed profile, sediment composition, and mud concentration. Runs 1–3 examined tidal ranges of 0.8, 1.5, and 3.0 m, representing microtidal, mesotidal, and macrotidal regimes, respectively. Because the study sites along the Pilbara coast of Western Australia are characterised by a mesotidal regime, a tidal range of 1.5 m was adopted for the subsequent scenarios.
Tidal asymmetry in Runs 4 and 5 was generated by combining the principal lunar semidiurnal constituent, M2, with its first overtide, M4. A relative phase difference of \(2\varphi_{M4} - \varphi_{M2}=90 ^\circ\) represented flood-dominant conditions, whereas a phase difference of \(270^\circ\) represented ebb-dominant condition. Here, \(\varphi_{M4}\) and \(\varphi_{M2}\) denote the phases of constituents M4 and M2, respectively. For simplicity, \(\varphi_{M2}=0^\circ\) in all scenarios
A gentle upper-intertidal slope of 0.035%, representing a convex-upward profile, was applied to the flood- and ebb-dominated conditions in Runs 6 and 7, respectively. The influence of sediment composition was examined in Runs 8 and 9, in which the mud fraction was increased to 20% and reduced to 0%, respectively. Run 9 therefore represented a purely sandy substrate. In Run 10, the suspended mud concentration at the boundary was increased from 5 to 10 mg L\(^{-1}\) to investigate the influence of sediment availability on tidal-flat morphology.
